# SLA Management

`customer_support.entitlement_and_sla.sla_management` · v1.0.0 · **draft**

**Which clock is running on this ticket, is it running for the right reason, and when does it run out?**


> Running the clocks that an entitlement created: knowing which clocks exist on a ticket, which one the ticket is actually judged on, when each started, whether it is legitimately running right now, and when it runs out in the customer's covered hours rather than the agent's. SLA management is bookkeeping in the honourable sense — the value is entirely in the ledger being true. It is not the work of avoiding a breach (that is breach_prevention, and it happens hours earlier), and it is not the promise itself (that is entitlement_verification, and it is a contract clause). A team that manages clocks well can still miss every deadline; a team that manages them badly cannot tell whether it missed them at all.

## Expertise applied


## Outcomes

- Every ticket under an entitlement carries an explicit clock state — running, paused, met or breached — and never an implied one.
- Every clock names the promise it measures: first response, next response, restoration or resolution. Which one the ticket is judged on is decided before the deadline, not after it.
- Every pause carries a recorded cause and a recorded restart condition, so the pause can be audited by someone who was not there.
- Deadlines are computed inside the entitlement's coverage window and quoted to the customer in the customer's local time.
- A breach is recorded as a breach. It is never dissolved by a retroactive pause, a reclassification or a merge.
- The deadline the customer believes in and the deadline the system holds are the same deadline.
- Attainment is reported next to the pause ratio, so nobody can read the first number without the number that qualifies it.


## Failure modes

- The pause as a parking space. The ticket is set waiting-on-customer with a question the customer has already answered, or with no question at all. The clock stops, the queue reports health, and the ticket rots in a state nobody looks at.
- Clock laundering. Reclassify, reassign, split or merge a ticket near its deadline and a fresh clock starts. The metric survives; the customer's wait does not reset.
- Measuring a promise the contract did not make — reporting resolution attainment when the entitlement promised first response, or the reverse. Everyone works the displayed clock, so displaying the wrong one is a team-wide error, not an individual one.
- First response satisfied by an autoresponder or a holding reply that says nothing specific about the ticket. Contractually a response, practically nothing, and once the field is satisfiable without reading the ticket the queue learns to satisfy it that way.
- Business-hours arithmetic done in the agent's timezone instead of the entitlement's coverage window. Produces real breaches over weekends and phantom breaches on public holidays that exist in one country and not another.
- Treating met as good. A met clock on a furious customer is a measurement failure — the promise being measured was not the promise they thought they had — and it is invisible to every SLA report ever built.
- Silent pauses. A clock stopped by a status change nobody intended as a pause, most often a bulk update, a merge or an automation firing on a stale rule.
- Internal waiting treated as customer waiting. Waiting on engineering is our problem; the moment it stops the clock, the queue shows a healthy board full of tickets nobody has touched in weeks.
- A breach discovered by the customer before it is discovered by the queue. The clock was arithmetically perfect and nobody was watching it.
- Per-ticket clocks during a widespread incident, so one fix breaches many clocks at once and generates a stack of individual apologies instead of one honest communication.
- Retroactive clock correction as routine practice. Correcting a genuinely wrong start is right; doing it monthly at reporting time means the ledger is now written by whoever runs the report.


## KPIs

| KPI | Unit | Direction | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| first_response_attainment | percent | higher_is_better | Share of tickets whose first-response clock was met. Uninterpretable without the pause ratio and the invalid-pause rate beside it, because both can manufacture it.  |
| resolution_attainment | percent | higher_is_better | Share of tickets whose resolution or restoration clock was met. |
| pause_ratio | percent | target_band | Share of elapsed wall time spent with the clock paused. The most diagnostic SLA metric there is and the one almost nobody reports. A band rather than a direction: near zero usually means agents are afraid to pause legitimately, and high means the queue is parking.  |
| invalid_pause_rate | percent | lower_is_better | Paused tickets with no live unanswered question to the customer. Measures the abuse directly instead of inferring it from attainment.  |
| breach_rate | percent | lower_is_better | Share of clocks missed. Read alongside breach severity — not all misses cost the same. |
| proactive_breach_disclosure_rate | percent | higher_is_better | Share of breaches the customer was told about before the deadline rather than after. The single best predictor of whether a breach becomes an escalation.  |
| met_but_dissatisfied_rate | percent | lower_is_better | Tickets that met every clock and still produced a detractor. The falsifier for attainment; without it the attainment number cannot be wrong and therefore cannot be informative.  |
| retroactive_clock_correction_rate | percent | lower_is_better | Clocks adjusted after the fact. Some correction is honest housekeeping; a rising rate means the ledger is being written by whoever runs the report.  |
| clock_coverage | percent | higher_is_better | Share of entitled tickets that actually carry a clock. Usually assumed to be complete and usually is not — untracked tickets are where the expensive breaches live.  |

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> This capability is deliberately narrow. It owns the state of the clock and the truthfulness of the ledger, and nothing else. Predicting and averting a miss is breach_prevention, which is a separate capability because that work happens hours before the deadline while nothing about the ticket looks different yet — an alert at the moment of breach is a notification about the past. Deciding what was promised is entitlement_verification. Saying the deadline to a human is expectation_setting.
Nothing here is executable against today's substrate: there is no ticket, SLA clock or entitlement fact path in the shipped packs, so every inference this capability wants sits in planned_substrate (sla.clock_state, sla.target_first_response_at, ticket.first_response_at, entitlement.coverage_hours) and in the pending L2 types sla_breach_imminent, sla_breached and first_response_overdue. That is the backlog, not a defect in this file.
